title: Babylon falls (Apocalypse 18)
hook: the merchants weep over a city built on luxury

segments.voice: Yesterday, the woman with the moon under her feet. Your line was clothed with the sun. Did you find the moon last night? Day six hundred twenty-eight.

Open a shopping app and scroll. Gold jewelry. Silk scarves. Rare wood furniture. Perfume. Fine wine. Imported spices. Grass-fed beef. A car. Everything delivered to your door, from somewhere you'll never see, made by people you'll never meet. Now read chapter eighteen of the Apocalypse, and you'll find almost the same list, nearly two thousand years old. Gold, silver, pearls, silk, scarlet, ivory, cinnamon, perfume, wine, oil, fine flour, cattle, horses, chariots. It's the shipping manifest of the greatest city in the world. And everyone who traded in it is standing at a distance, crying, because the city is gone.
screen: `SCROLLING A SHOPPING APP.` → `THE SAME LIST, 2,000 YEARS OLD.` → `THE CITY IS GONE.`

segments.voice: Babylon had fallen centuries before John was born. In the Apocalypse it's a code name, and most scholars and much of the Christian tradition read it as Rome, the city on seven hills, rich, powerful, and hard on the people who wouldn't bow to it. The first letter of Peter seems to use the same code, sending greetings from the church in Babylon. In chapter eighteen an angel lights up the earth with his glory and cries out, in the Douay-Rheims: "Babylon the great is fallen, is fallen." Then a voice from heaven: "Go out from her, my people; that you be not partakers of her sins." And then three groups of mourners. Kings, who lived in luxury with her. Merchants, who got rich off her. Sailors, who carried her cargo. They all stand far off, afraid, saying the same thing: in one hour. In one hour her judgment came; in one hour her riches were laid waste. Three times the text says it. Listen to the merchants' list again, all the way to the end. After the horses and chariots, the last items are bodies and human souls. People, bought and sold like the cinnamon. That's what the luxury was standing on. Then an angel picks up a stone like a great millstone and throws it into the sea: like that, Babylon will be thrown down and found no more. No more music in her streets. No more lamps. No more bride and bridegroom. The chapter isn't against beauty or trade. It's about a whole way of life that forgot people were not merchandise, and how fast it can vanish. Catholic social teaching has long made the same warning.
screen: `BABYLON: A CODE NAME FOR ROME.` · `GO OUT FROM HER, MY PEOPLE.` · `IN ONE HOUR, LAID WASTE.` · `THE LIST ENDS WITH HUMAN SOULS.` · then, large: `BABYLON THE GREAT IS FALLEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: buy one fewer thing. Sit comfortably and breathe. Bring to mind the last few things you bought or were about to buy. Picture them in a row. Pick one you don't really need, the one that was more about the scroll than the need. Now imagine not buying it. Notice whether anything in you protests, and let it protest. Then think about who made the things you do buy: the hands, the fields, the factories, the drivers. If you pray, you can pray for them. If you don't, just hold them in mind for a moment, people, not merchandise. The bell holds the time.
Babylon falls. Apocalypse eighteen: the great city of luxury, built on bought and sold lives, laid waste in one hour. Today's word.
Your line: what doesn't last. Today, skip the purchase you chose, and give the money or the time to someone who needs it. Day six hundred twenty-eight.

screen: `DAY 628 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE SUPPER OF THE LAMB.`

howItsDone: Catholic social teaching warns against consumerism and insists that people are never merchandise; many Catholics practice simplicity through fasting and almsgiving, especially in Lent, and support fair labor and the fight against human trafficking.

fork.setup: you live in the great city. the voice from heaven says something about your life there. what does it say?
options: stay and enjoy it while it lasts.
go out from her, my people, so you don't share in her sins.

fork.reveal: go out from her, my people. not a call to leave a map location, many readers say, but to stop living by the city's values.

original.note: Greek: fallen, fallen is Babylon the great (Apocalypse 18:2), echoing Isaiah 21:9.

trapdoor: what you thought: a prophecy about a future city's destruction.
what it means: a picture of a whole economy of luxury, built on people bought and sold, and how fast it can vanish.
what a scholar hears: Babylon as code for Rome (compare 1 Peter 5:13); the cargo list (18:12–13) mirrors Roman imports and ends with 'bodies and souls of men'.
